task.title: Named strings
task.shortdesc: A named string saves text from an element so that you can use it elsewhere, such as in a running header or footer. string-set saves the text and string() retrieves it.

context.p: The element names in the examples, such as title and h1, are placeholders. Use the names that occur in your XML.

info.p: The string-set property takes none, which is the initial value, or a comma-separated list of assignments. Each assignment is a name that you choose, followed by what to save.
Each h1 element saves its text in chapter-title. When a later h1 is found, it replaces the saved value. One declaration can save several strings:
What to save is a list of one or more of these items, joined in order:

ul.li: content() gives text of the element. content(text), which is the default, gives the text of the element and its descendants, with white space collapsed. content(before) and content(after) give the text generated by ::before and ::after. content(first-letter) gives the first letter.
attr(name) gives the value of an attribute of the element. attr(name, "fallback") gives the fallback when the attribute is missing.

counter(name) gives the value of the innermost counter with that name. counters(name, ".") gives the values of all the counters with that name, from the outermost, joined with the string. Both accept a counter style as the last argument, such as upper-roman.

info.p: This XML and stylesheet save the text, a prefix and an attribute of a title:
The left margin shows "Chapter A-4" and the right margin shows "Install the package". For a title without a code attribute, the left margin shows "Chapter No code".

A string is saved where the box of its element starts, or where it would start if the element has display: none. That is why a page can show different values of the same string, depending on which elements it contains.
Use string(name) in the content property of a page-margin box. The name is the one you wrote in string-set. An optional second argument chooses which value to use on the page.

ul.li: first is the first value saved on the page. If the page does not save one, it is the value in effect at the end of the previous page. This is the default.
start is the value in effect at the top of the page. It is empty if the string has not been saved yet.
last is the value in effect at the end of the page.
first-except works like first, but is empty on a page that saves the string. It is useful to hide a running header on the page where a chapter starts.
